endorsements.quote: Users will receive training addressing: explainability, usability, alerts and the strengths and weaknesses of the AI-CDSS.

While using AI-CDSS, it was felt that HCPs must apply their clinical judgement to each situation, as they alone have the necessary scientific, ethical and moral understanding and are ultimately legally accountable for their decisions [ 10 ].
Independent stakeholders should be involved in auditing and ensuring that these standards are met.
AI-CDSS will be evaluated against both human performance and ideal outcomes.
AI-CDSS will comply with all relevant regulatory guidelines.

AI-CDSS developers will be transparent about what data they have used and their bias mitigation strategies.
Developers will be clear and specific about the proposed purpose and scope of their AI-CDSS.
Use of a certainty index as well as further research into how user biases and decision making context affect AI-CDSS use
AI-CDSS output will be continually monitored with multi- disciplinary oversight, and users can report on usability, accuracy, errors and impact to developers.

Impose detailed implementation plans with sufficient training and education regarding the benefits, drawback and scope of functionality of the AI-CDSS.
Alert systems must be regularly assessed so they prioritise significant alerts and minimise low importance notifications

unlisted_practices: Develop AI-CDSS from evidence-based research using datasets representative of the patients on whom the tool will be applied.
Co-develop AI-CDSS with clinician and patient input.
Store patient data safely and securely, installing AI-CDSS on secure systems with appropriate data security.
Appoint local champions who receive additional training, advocate for the software and provide continuing help to staff.
Give users options on how they integrate AI into their practice, including customisable alert settings and personalisable interfaces.
Make explanations of the AI-CDSS available to users if they desire them.
Tailor explainability to the function of the AI-CDSS and the needs of its users rather than requiring uniform explainability.
Test AI-CDSS performance for bias on relevant subsets of the population and account for imbalances in training data.
Follow rigorous data management practices and use data lineage to trace data origins.
Hold regular meetings between clinicians and developers to keep AI-CDSS responsive to clinical needs.
Invest in reliable, high-speed networks with backup systems and secure offline functionality for AI-CDSS.
Ensure HCPs still discuss AI results and decision making with patients.
Involve a multidisciplinary team including developers, clinicians, patients and administrative staff in planning AI-CDSS integration.
Train users so they are made aware of where legal accountability lies and of potential legal risks of using AI-CDSS.

screen.reason: This paper presents a framework and consensus recommendations (the 'Hippocratic Oath for AI') derived from an expert workshop/focus groups to address challenges in implementing AI-based clinical decision support systems.
